column2: “I just remembered something awful. Your favorite S-rank student… He seemed extremely disappointed with his answers. So after saying ‘I don’t know,’ he said he was giving up and walked straight out.” Aki and Ye Sheng looked at each other.
“But he answered so well! Why would he give up?” Professor Guderian looked ready to leap into the air.
“With those questions and those answers…” Ye Sheng shrugged with a wry smile. “You might be the only person who thinks he did well.”
“We must fix this! We have to get him back! I’ll call his family!” Professor Guderian patted himself all over, searching for his phone.
Ye Sheng scratched his head and sighed. “Let me call… You’ll frighten his family like this. They’ll think you’re up to something.”
Three in the morning. In the dead silence, a telephone rang down the hallway of Lu Mingfei’s home.
His aunt jolted upright from sleep and turned toward the phone on the nightstand, which was ringing so merrily it almost seemed to be jumping up and down.
“Did someone in your family die? Calling in the middle of the night!” She snatched it up and shouted furiously.
Soon, the anger left her face. She couldn’t say a word. Her husband sat up in bed and saw his wife, hair disheveled, eyes vacant, as though she had been struck by lightning.
The ringing next door woke Lu Mingze, too. He turned toward the other bed and saw his older cousin licking his lips in his sleep, making happy little piglike grunts.
The following morning. The Regent Hotel.

The whole family had turned out for the VIP dining lounge on the ninth-floor executive level. His uncle, in an immaculate suit, stuck out his belly and lectured the boys about behaving properly in a high-class place and not constantly touching the cutlery. His aunt looked around, clicking her tongue in admiration. A high-class hotel really was high-class.
“Mr. Lu Mingfei? Green tea or dark tea?” A neatly dressed waiter approached and addressed Lu Mingfei, sandwiched between his uncle and aunt.
“What are the prices?” His uncle displayed the air of a man accustomed to fine establishments.
“Everything is complimentary for guests in the presidential suite. That is the suite Professor Guderian has booked.”
“American schools really are rich!” His aunt acquired an instant respect for Cassell College.

With a ding, the express elevator opened. A burly, gray-haired old man strode toward their table by the window, Ye Sheng on his left and Aki Sakatoku on his right. Flanked by the handsome young man and lovely young woman like a hunter with hound and hawk, he cut a commanding figure. Without a word of preamble, he seized Lu Mingfei’s hand. “Hello, Lu Mingfei!”
“Hello… Professor… Guderian?” Lu Mingfei was embarrassed by this overwhelming enthusiasm. “Your Chinese is really good.”

Professor Guderian’s eyes lit up. He scratched his head happily. “Is it that good? I learned from CCTV’s evening news. We promote Chinese throughout the college. Everyone knows China is going to become the most prosperous place in the world!” He looked at Lu Mingfei, eyes shining, openly trying to win him over. “Join us. You won’t need English. Every student speaks Chinese.”

Lu Mingfei blinked. What did that mean? Chinese? No need for English? In a life with so few bright spots, that TOEFL score was about the only thing he had to show. If even his one bright spot didn’t matter, what did Cassell College see in him? Professor Guderian, whom he had just met, looked positively overjoyed.
“Hello, Professor Gu. I’m Lu Mingfei’s uncle.” Unable to bear being left out, his uncle squeezed between them.
Unable to remember the whole name Guderian, he had very cleverly shortened it to Professor Gu.
“You two really don’t look alike!” Professor Guderian shook his hand.
Now it was his uncle’s turn to be embarrassed. For all his grandeur and his presidential suite, this Professor Guderian seemed a little out of touch.
Behind him, Ye Sheng tugged his sleeve. The three of them sat across the table.
“Let’s have breakfast.” Professor Guderian took his fork in his left hand and knife in his right, never taking his eyes off Lu Mingfei.
Lu Mingfei felt he was being watched with the anticipation of a gourmet regarding a roast chicken.

The expensive breakfast included salmon rolls and freshly squeezed lemon juice, and the solid-silver cutlery was decidedly impressive. It immediately banished his uncle’s displeasure. After all, there was nothing shameful about Lu Mingfei not looking like him. Hosts and guests alike were happy.

Professor Guderian praised Lu Mingfei’s outstanding interview performance. His uncle was delighted to say that you could tell at a glance Cassell College was an American school for the elite. Chinese universities simply couldn’t compare with such style.

Ye Sheng had prepared thoroughly. He produced a copy of the college’s official registration with the U.S. Department of Education for his aunt to inspect, followed by a photo album. This was the library; this was the sports center; this was the concert hall. The campus in the pictures was elegant and old-fashioned, like a completely renovated castle.

One photo showed Ye Sheng himself on a windsurfing board, a sea of sails competing behind him. It was the annual college windsurfing race, he explained. Cassell had beaten the University of Chicago three years running.
His aunt was won over, too. She exclaimed that their Mingfei must have earned extraordinary blessings in a previous life to attend such a school.

Lu Mingfei had a strange feeling. It was like marrying off a daughter. He was the daughter who cost money at home but would bring in a bride-price if married out. The groom’s family was eager, and the bride’s family was more than happy to oblige.
He worked up his courage. “Professor Guderian… what does your college see in me?”

“Your overall qualities! Your enormous potential!” The professor didn’t look remotely as though he were joking. “We think so highly of you that we want not only to admit you, but to give you a scholarship. I’ve decided to allocate thirty-six thousand U.S. dollars a year from the scholarship fund under my name. Enough to see you through all four years!”
His uncle and aunt gasped together.
“Professor Gu… there aren’t… any conditions attached, are there? Like having to pay it back afterward… We should be clear about that first.” His uncle sensed something wrong.
“No! Absolutely not! A scholarship is a reward for your nephew, because he is outstanding!” Professor Guderian declared with righteous conviction.
“That sounds fake.” His uncle shook his head.

“Of course, there are other reasons. Lu Mingfei’s parents happen to be honorary alumni, and they have made donations to the college. All other things being equal, we give preference to alumni’s children.”

Lu Mingfei looked up at once. It felt as though a small rabbit were jumping in his chest. He had forgotten how long it had been since he had heard any real news of his parents. His mother’s letters only told him to take care of himself and study hard, the same thing every time. Sometimes he felt those letters were just a way of brushing him off, and his parents no longer cared about him at all.

“They care about you very much,” Professor Guderian said. “I haven’t met them myself, but I hear they’ve been working on a very important research project, traveling all over the world these past years. I have a photograph of them here. Oh, and a letter your mother wrote to the college about you.”

He took a photograph from his pocket and placed it before Lu Mingfei. It showed a summer garden. In the distance was what looked like Cassell College in the sunset. Closer were walls of climbing greenery, a deep, luminous green. A man and a woman walked hand in hand among them. The man wore a loose white shirt, wide-legged trousers, and wooden sandals. The woman wore a plain white cotton house dress.

Lu Mingfei reached out and gently touched the two faces. That handsome man and beautiful woman were his parents, but they were so far away, in some corner of the world he could never reach. His nose began to sting. In the photograph, they were looking into each other’s faces, smiling warmly. Clearly, it was their own little world for two. They had probably forgotten that, between them, they had once made a child.
His aunt offered a concise assessment. “Two people their age, still so romantic!”
Professor Guderian passed him a letter next. It was short and printed out, probably an email:
Dear Principal Anjou:
It has been a long time since we were in touch. I hope you are as well as ever.
We probably will not be able to meet for quite some time. There have been new developments in our research, and we cannot leave.

There is something I would like to ask of you. My son Lu Mingfei is now eighteen. He is a clever child. His grades may not be especially good, but we both believe he can accomplish something in scholarship. If possible, please help him gain admission to Cassell College.
Since I cannot tell him in person, please pass on a message for me: his mother and father love him.
Yours sincerely,
Qiao Weini
Lu Mingfei read in silence. For a long time, he said nothing.
Professor Guderian cleared his throat. Then, looking straight into Lu Mingfei’s eyes, he said with immense tenderness and slightly imperfect pronunciation, “Mingfei, Mommy and Daddy love you.”
Lu Mingfei stared, completely stunned.
“The principal insisted that I pass on your parents’ message. He cares about you very much, too,” Professor Guderian said.

The clumsy delivery was too much for Lu Mingze, who burst out laughing. His parents couldn’t keep straight faces either. In the letter, Qiao Weini’s words were so tender they could have brought tears to your eyes. Spoken by a gray-haired, gray-bearded Professor Guderian with his clueless expression, they acquired an irresistibly comic incongruity. Ye Sheng and Aki Sakatoku shook their heads with helpless smiles. The professor reached out and gave Lu Mingfei a hearty pat on the shoulder.
The atmosphere at the table suddenly grew much warmer.
“I’m going to the restroom.” Lu Mingfei stood.
He leaned his back against the restroom door and stood quietly for a while. Tears began to run silently down his face.
They had all laughed, but he couldn’t see anything funny about it.

It should have been moving. Through all those years, all the way to eighteen, hardly anyone had cared what he thought or what he did. Time after time, he had walked home from school and watched his classmates get picked up, one by one. Looking back at the dust those cars left behind, he had sometimes thought that perhaps no one in this world loved him at all.
“Mingfei, Mommy and Daddy love you.”
Lu Mingfei believed it. On paper, the words hadn’t really made him feel anything. But when Professor Guderian said them aloud, suddenly he believed.
“I love you.” Words like that had to be spoken. Saying them was different from writing them on paper. Especially to a drooping little kid starved of love.

He knew he was being rather stupid, but he couldn’t help the sadness. He could only hide in the restroom. He slid down against the door and squatted, tears streaming, drawing circles on the tiles. He would wait until the tears stopped, then go out and say he had needed to take a dump.
Just then, a pair of running shoes with a muted purple pattern appeared before him.

He looked up in surprise. A girl stood there. From the bottom up: running shoes, close-fitting jeans, a little white tank top beneath a cropped blue-striped shirt, and a baseball cap perched on her head.
Something seemed wrong. He couldn’t work out what. He blinked.
The tall, radiant girl looked down at him sidelong. Sterling-silver four-leaf-clover earrings swayed at her ears, their tiny diamonds flashing painfully bright.
“This is the ladies’ room,” she informed him at her leisure.
Lu Mingfei returned to the table with his head hanging. The pretty, tall girl followed, her face cold.

“Oh? Nono, I thought you’d gone out to have fun.” Professor Guderian stood. “Let me introduce Chen Motong, a second-year student of Chinese descent and our student interviewer for this visit. This is your new schoolmate, Lu Mingfei.”
“Nono?” Lu Mingfei paused. The name sounded familiar.
“I ate at a street-food stall last night, and my stomach’s been a little upset. I’ve been in the restroom.” Chen Motong sat beside Aki Sakatoku.
“Why didn’t you invite me? I’d love to try one of those things called street-food stalls.” Professor Guderian sounded disappointed. “I’ve heard about them on the news.”
“In a report about recycled gutter oil, was it?” Chen Motong picked up her knife and fork and stole the last salmon roll from Ye Sheng’s plate.
“I have one left, too. You can have it.” Aki Sakatoku forked hers onto Chen Motong’s plate as well.
“You work together so well. Just like a married couple. Why haven’t you gotten married yet?” Chen Motong mumbled around a mouthful of salmon roll.
Ye Sheng and Aki Sakatoku looked at each other, both a little helpless and a little embarrassed.

Lu Mingfei was grateful that the girl hadn’t exposed his humiliation. But as soon as she joined them, the warm family atmosphere evaporated. Sitting closest to the window, Chen Motong looked at no one and buttered her bread by herself. In the sunlight, her long hair glowed a deep red, like wine.

He had never met a girl like her. She wasn’t like Su Xiaoqiang, who cared so much about how others saw her. Nor was she like the delicate, quiet Chen Wenwen, who avoided people’s eyes. Chen Motong looked like a proud princess who didn’t care about anything. Even when she looked straight at you, you felt that she wasn’t really seeing you at all.
His uncle was stealing looks at her wrist. Lu Mingfei knew what he was looking at: the silver, diamond-set Omega watch.
“Mind if I eat yours, too?” Chen Motong wiped her mouth with a napkin and fixed her eyes on Lu Mingfei.
He could only nod. What a rare honor: such a proud princess actually looking into his eyes and speaking to him… for the sake of a salmon roll.
“Nono, some manners. Look after our new student,” Professor Guderian said.
“He has no appetite.” She glanced at Lu Mingfei. “Look how distracted he is. He could probably even walk into the wrong restroom.”
His heart gave a jolt. Chen Motong stuck out her tongue and took his entire breakfast plate.
“Oh? Really? Mingfei, is there anything you’re still worried about?” Professor Guderian looked into his eyes. “An opportunity to attend Cassell College is extremely rare. You must treasure it!”
“I… I still need to think.” He lowered his head.

His uncle, aunt, and Lu Mingze were dumbfounded. Had something short-circuited in his brain? A free meal had fallen from the sky. What was there to think about? Other people couldn’t get such an opportunity however hard they begged. He should just open his mouth and catch it.
Professor Guderian grew anxious. “If there are any conditions we can meet, just name them!”
“No.” Lu Mingfei shook his head. “I…”

“It’s his first love.” Chen Motong twirled her fork, Lu Mingfei’s salmon roll speared on it. “Let me think. White… long hair… very gentle… quiet… a hundred sixty-five centimeters tall… a girl in his class. Yes, more or less. Someone like that.”
She turned to the window and chewed as though no one else existed.
Lu Mingfei shuddered. Lu Mingze’s ears pricked up. His uncle and aunt gave him suspicious looks. The table fell silent. The only sound, extraordinarily clear, was Chen Motong chewing his salmon roll.
“Nono, stop it,” Aki Sakatoku said.

“Just kidding.” Chen Motong pushed away the empty plate, showed her bright white teeth, and gave Lu Mingfei a beautiful, unfriendly smile. “We hardly know each other. We only met today, didn’t we? Even if he had a first love, how would I know who she was?”
Everyone exhaled together. Professor Guderian looked immensely relieved.

“Our Mingfei wouldn’t get involved with girls. Would you, Mingfei?” His aunt was reassured. He hadn’t secretly found a girlfriend behind her back, which meant her authority in the household remained intact. Besides, she rather doubted anyone could be blind enough to fall for him. The girls at his school were all well-brought-up young ladies. What chance did he have?
“Who’d want me?” Lu Mingfei chewed and chewed a stalk of asparagus. As long as his mouth kept moving, he didn’t have to fake an expression.
“A student’s priority should be studying,” his uncle said.
“You’re teching to tier three,” Chen Motong suddenly said.
His heart trembled. The asparagus fell onto his plate.
Late at night, in the quiet, Lu Mingfei sat at his laptop with two things open: QQ and StarCraft.
His uncle and aunt had spent the day scolding him for not knowing a good thing when he saw one. No matter how Professor Guderian pleaded or persuaded, he had insisted he needed to think.
“What’s there to think about? Still hoping for Harvard, are you?” His aunt had finally snorted in contempt.
Chen Motong had been right. It was because of Chen Wenwen.

He had read a StarCraft story called “The Bloodstained Totem,” about a giant robot fighting on another planet that secretly used the military network to chat on QQ with a little girl on Earth. Under low, lead-gray clouds, the robot, named Godzilla, fought Zerg through hails of bullets while exchanging warm little messages with the girl.
One day, Godzilla told her on QQ, I’m going to die. All my battery fluid’s leaked out. I’m running out of power.
The girl said, You’re funny. You really think you’re a giant robot? If you don’t feel like talking, just say so. See you tomorrow.
Godzilla said, Talking with you feels so nice.
Then it was forced offline. On a distant planet, an angry Zergling leaped onto the wreck of a giant robot and tore through its circuits with sharp claws.

Lu Mingfei felt he was that giant robot, and Chen Wenwen was the little girl. Sometimes she told him very private things, and he was happy, replying with all sorts of cute emojis to show he was listening carefully. But she never understood why he did it, and didn’t know that he waited for her on QQ, hour after hour. If one day the circuits inside the giant robot called Lu Mingfei failed, would Chen Wenwen feel sad?
The more he thought about it, the sadder he became. It was a tragic feeling: battery fluid leaking through his chest, circuits crackling all over his body.

The literary club’s group chat was silent. Without Chen Wenwen, no one would ever discuss literature. The beauty of literature was mainly a matter of the beauty of the muse. The muse sat in the sunlight in a white cotton dress, her long hair loose. That was the beauty of literature.
In the StarCraft channel, Old Tang was imparting secret techniques to a crowd. Ever since defeating Lu Mingfei, he had styled himself the channel’s top player.
The big-faced cat avatar flashed. Nono was online.
Lu Mingfei hesitated. “It was you?”
“Yeah. Chen Motong.” Her reply felt lazy. “Nothing to do, so I came on for a couple of games.”
“How did you know my ID?”
“Crowdsourced stalking. Heh. You actually use an ID like ‘Mingming.’ Sounds like a girl. And ‘Sunset’s Imprint’… Are you pretending to be a girl online?”
“You could even dig that up? Keep it secret, please. That’s just me messing with my cousin.”
“Kidding. Norma found it. A piece of cake for her. You’re pretty good at StarCraft.”
“Come on. I lost to you.”
“I lost. Norma was playing with me. We both controlled the same side. At the end, I knew you were teching to tier three because she secretly revealed the map and saw it.”
“May every cheater’s whole family drop dead!” Lu Mingfei typed.
It was automatic. Everyone tossed that line around in the group. Nobody took it seriously.
“I’m the only one in my family,” Nono replied.
Lu Mingfei paused. “Sorry.”
“What’s there to be sorry about?” Her reply was flat. “Want a game?”
“Not in the mood.”
“Girl broke your heart?”
A shiver ran through him. Nono was like a little witch, seeing through everything about him, leaving him nowhere to hide.
“Not yet… I don’t have a girlfriend, so obviously my heart isn’t broken. What do you want from me, big sis?” he typed.
“‘Big sis.’ That’s sweet.” Nono sent a toothy grin. “Come on, tell me what’s going on. Maybe I can help.”
“How could you help? You don’t even know her.”
“No, I don’t know Chen Wenwen.” The little witch replied instantly.
“How much do you actually know?” Lu Mingfei was suddenly terrified.
“Too much.”
“Who… are you people?” His hands were shaking a little.

“Suspicious, right? Your parents haven’t been home in six years, then suddenly recommend you to an American college. Your grades are average… no, actually, they’re terrible, but the college gives you a huge scholarship. You clearly talked complete nonsense in the interview, but the interviewers say your answers were wonderful. Compared with that, knowing who you have a crush on is nothing.”
“Yeah. Only my uncle and aunt don’t suspect anything. They think my parents can do anything. All the way home, they kept asking how to get my cousin sent abroad, too.”
“Beg me! Beg, and I’ll tell you things. Like… what Chen Wenwen’s thinking…” The little witch’s evil nature was stirring again.
“You know?”
“A woman’s intuition tells me…”
“What?”
“She doesn’t like you.”
“Get lost!”

Lu Mingfei didn’t believe it. He remembered that afternoon when only he and Chen Wenwen had been in the classroom. He was wiping the blackboard. She sat on the teaching platform in a white cotton dress, sneakers, and white ankle socks, humming softly. The slanting evening sun shone on the newly replaced desks. Virginia creeper hung down outside the window. In that evening between spring and summer, everything was especially still. Suddenly, Chen Wenwen had turned and asked, Lu Mingfei, would you like to join our literary club?

He had felt petrified, only his heart still hammering. Outside, flowers and grass grew wild, the sun sank, the cicadas seemed to sing a hundred times faster. Time slipped through his fingers, the hours changed, yet the gaze between him and Chen Wenwen seemed eternal.
“Just kidding. Come on, let me advise you. Have you ever given her flowers?” Nono asked.
“Does foxtail grass count?” He perked up and began talking nonsense again.
“Taken her to a movie?”
“When the school screened revolutionary films for educational purposes, I sat next to her at Sparkling Red Star.”
“When’s her birthday?”
“October tenth.”
“Ever given her a birthday present?”
“She borrowed my pen to write back to the boys who sent her birthday cards. Then she didn’t return it. The next day she said it could count as my present…”
“Could you be any more hopeless?”
“I don’t think so.”

“You’re a disgrace to Cassell College!” Nono was angry. “Come on. Let your senior teach you a thing or two. First, you have to pursue a girl! If you don’t make a move, do you expect her to confess to you? Second, what matters most to a girl is feeling happy and cherished. Have you ever tried making Chen Wenwen feel that way?”
“Happy and cherished?” He stared.

“For example, suppose—and this is only hypothetical—Chen Wenwen really likes you, but you don’t feel anything for her. Then one day you fail an exam and feel utterly miserable. Suddenly, there she is, picking you up in a Ferrari. In front of everyone, she strokes your hair and says, ‘There, there. Don’t worry. You’ll do better next time.’ Wouldn’t you practically explode with happiness? Even if you didn’t like her before, wouldn’t you fall into her arms on the spot?”
“Immediately! No hesitation! I’d put a leash around my own neck and run after her barking!” Lu Mingfei answered with absolute conviction.
“Hopeless! That makes you look way too easy. At least squirm a little and pretend to resist!”
“Senior… what should I do, then?” He was entirely sincere about becoming her pupil.

“Burn your boats! Tell everyone you like her. Say it loud. Gamble your dignity as a man and your future on it. Do you understand girls? No girl will really hate a boy for a confession honest and brave enough. Even if she doesn’t accept, she’ll remember you.”
“What if she doesn’t accept?”
“Fly to America with your beautiful memories of heartbreak.”
“That sounds pretty tragic…”

“Loving someone isn’t easy. You have to fight your way through an army! The last Zergling, racing through the fire of countless Dragoons, down to its final hit point, slashes out with one claw and turns the battle! If you die halfway, that’s natural enough. But a Zergling that won’t charge into the guns isn’t a good Zergling!” Nono said.

Lu Mingfei paused. He felt the killing intent in her words, and that beautiful, indifferent face suddenly appeared before him. That girl like a blade of steel… Now she had swung it, cutting straight into his heart, blood splashing everywhere. In that instant, he made the boldest decision of his eighteen years. He would be the Zergling that charged into the guns. In those final three months before graduation, the last time he and Chen Wenwen would be classmates, he would tell her he had liked her for three years. However feeble that final swipe, whether or not it broke through her defenses, he was determined to be a good Zergling!
“Understood!” he said.

“Bring flowers. If you don’t know what she likes, go with roses. Deep red. No girl really dislikes roses. Have moving music in the background. Most importantly, say it in front of everyone. That shows your courage!” Nono said. “Good luck, little bro!”
“Yes, ma’am!” He imagined a mighty female general issuing orders to him, her foot soldier.
“But… if you succeed, the road to Cassell College will close to you forever!”
With that, Nono logged off, giving him no chance to reply.

Lu Mingfei tipped back his head and let out a long breath. He was eager to try, convinced that this bold confession would succeed. Giving up America for it was nothing. He would never see Nono again, though. That was a slight regret. He felt he would miss her. Before Nono, no girl had ever burst into his world with such ferocity. Not even Chen Wenwen.

He looked at the gray big-faced cat avatar, no longer bouncing, and suddenly felt it was a kind of magic. The moment his confession succeeded, Cassell College, Professor Guderian, and Nono would vanish from this world like bubbles.
In a suite on the Regent Hotel’s executive floor, Nono sipped her coffee at ease.
QQ was still open on her Apple laptop. She had merely set herself to invisible. Lu Mingfei’s final message arrived: a simple “Thank you.”

In another chat window, someone with the ID “Sonic” said, “What are you doing? Teaching him how to confess to a girl? If our S-rank gives up the gate to Cassell for love, the principal will go insane.”

“Are you nuts? I’m just messing with him.” Nono wrinkled her delicate nose and smiled coldly. “How could that kind of confession work? Chen Wenwen’s a literary girl. If she likes someone, she’ll accept him. If she doesn’t, she won’t care how much he offers. Music, roses, and shouting ‘I love you’ are supposed to do it? Please!”
“Could you be any more immoral?”
“No.” Nono shrugged. “I have to admit, this is the most immoral thing I’ve ever done.”
“Why pick on a freshman?”
“A freshman? He’s S-rank! You and I are only A-rank. If we don’t bully him while we have the chance, it’ll be harder once he gets to college,” Nono said.

“Let’s hope nothing unexpected happens. Suppose Chen Wenwen’s just as secretly passionate as he is. She’s liked him for three years but won’t say it, and all they’re missing is a confession. Then you’ll have ruined everything.”
Nono stuck out her tongue. “Surely I can’t be that unlucky?”
“The Student Council needs someone like him. The only S-rank. We absolutely can’t let the Lionheart Society get him!” Sonic said.
“Nono.” Ye Sheng opened the door and poked his head in. “Professor Guderian wants you to join the discussion.”
“Oh.” She slipped on her cotton slippers and trotted out, holding her coffee cup.
In the outer room, Professor Guderian, Ye Sheng, and Aki Sakatoku sat around a coffee table, looking rather grave. A freshly printed document lay on the table.

“Nono, I have an assignment. I can only entrust it to you.” Professor Guderian picked up the document. “The college just faxed us the profile of a Russian candidate who appears to have an excellent bloodline. I must fly to Beijing at once and connect to Russia. I’m leaving the rest of Lu Mingfei’s enrollment to you.”
“Me?” Nono stared. “What about Ye Sheng and Aki?”

“Operation Kuimen has been moved forward. The principal will soon be coming to China in person. Professor Mans has ordered us to report to Sichuan immediately,” Ye Sheng said. “Aki and I still need some time for coordination training.”
“Is it really that urgent?” Nono pouted. At moments like this, she still looked like a child.

“When it’s your turn to carry out an operation, you’ll understand. You can’t wait an hour, or even a minute.” Ye Sheng patted her shoulder. “Miss certain moments once, and you might as well have missed an entire lifetime.”
